item.title: Bitcoin extends losses as growth concerns increase amid stock market rout. What could change the trend?
item.description:
Bitcoin extended the losses further yesterday following another rout in the stock market as growth concerns increased and the risk sentiment remained negative.

The market is seeing a slowdown in the economy in the next 6-12 months caused by Fed tightening, prolonged US-Iran stalemate, limited fiscal impulse due to the Democratic Congress and AI bubble burst.

This is a very negative macro backdrop that is likely to keep weighing on Bitcoin and the crypto market in general. Only a dovish Fed or a surprising breakthrough in the US-Iran situation are likely to reverse the current trend.

Next week, there’s only the US Flash PMIs as an important catalyst to watch. Weak data could exacerbate growth concerns and put further pressure on Bitcoin. Strong data, on the other hand, could trigger a short-term relief rally, although it wouldn’t change the bigger picture.

Of course, the focus will also be on US-Iran developments as an end to the war should lead to a positive repricing in growth expectations.

 

BITCOIN TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that Bitcoinbroke below the support zone around the 62,400 level, opening the door for a move into the 58,000 support next. If the price gets there, we can expect the buyers to step in, with a defined risk below the support, to position for a rally into the major downward trendline around the 74,000 level. The sellers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking lower to increase the bearish bets into the 50,000 level next.

BITCOIN TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 4 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 4 hour chart, we have a minor downward trendline defining the bearish momentum. If we get a pullback into the trendline, we can expect the sellers to lean on it, with a defined risk above it, to keep pushing into new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will look for a break higher to increase the bullish bets into the major downward trendline next.

On the 1 hour chart, we have another minor trendline that could act as resistance. The sellers will likely lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to keep targeting the 58,000 support. The buyers, on the other hand, will look for a break higher to extend the pullback into the next trendline. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

UPCOMING CATALYSTS

Today we have Trump speaking at a press conference about his Asia trip, but he could certainly digress and talk about Iran. On Monday, we get the US Flash PMIs. On Thursday, we get the latest US Jobless Claims figures. The focus will remain on growth concerns, the Fed and US-Iran developments.

item.title: Gold's panic selling signals capitulation, but a catalyst is needed for a bottom
item.description:
Gold extended the selloff further despite no changes in the fundamentals. In fact, the US dollar remained relatively flat, real yields fell a bit and rate hike expectations actually eased following another rout in the stock market.

This mix would generally support gold, but it looks like we got another liquidation caused by stock market losses.

To understand the mechanics, imagine that an investment fund holds stocks, gold and government bonds. Some stocks suddenly crash, and the fund suffers losses on leveraged positions. The fund may need to raise cash to meet margin calls, reduce leverage or satisfy investor redemptions. Rather than selling only the assets that caused the losses, it may sell whatever it can liquidate quickly. Gold is particularly useful in this situation because it is highly liquid and can be sold quickly.

The hawkish repricing is now over, and we might even see a dovish repricing in the next months if the equity losses extend further and economic data deteriorates. Therefore, the risk-reward for more downside has weakened, although we haven’t got any bullish catalyst yet to position for a reversal. Waiting for catalysts is always better than trying to catch falling knives.

On Monday, we get the Flash US PMIs. The data might provide the first bullish catalyst if it surprises to the downside as growth concerns may increase further and rate hike bets further down the curve should be unwound. A strong report, though, might add some more downward pressure.

What are FX option expiries?

The FX option expiration price levels refer to the strike prices where option contracts are set to expire. These levels include both calls and puts.

When you see "EUR/USD at 1.1600 for €4 billion" it means there is a total of €4 billion worth of options (calls + puts combined) that have a strike price of 1.1600 and are expiring at that specific time (the "New York Cut" at 10:00 AM ET).

Traders watch these levels because they often act as a "magnet" for the price. For example, if there's nothing happening in the market and the price is close to the expiry level, let's say 30-50 pips away, what you will usually see is the price moving into the expiry level. This happens due to the hedging activity of the market makers (banks, dealers and so on).

As the price gets closer to the strike price near expiration, these market makers must aggressively buy or sell the currency to hedge their risk. This hedging activity tends to suppress volatility and keep the price "pinned" close to the strike price until the expiration time passes.

EUROPEAN SESSION

In the European session, the main highlight was the UK Retail Sales report. The data showed a strong rebound in October, beating expectations across both headline and underlying measures, with volumes rising 0.7% m/m and sales excluding autos and fuel increasing 0.9%. The recovery was broad-based, supported by stronger food and non-food sales, while online spending also continued to expand.

Although the figures point to resilient consumer demand, the three-month growth rate remained relatively modest at 0.4%. Overall, the report does little to change the Bank of England policy outlook, with markets already expecting a 25 bps rate hike in December.

AMERICAN SESSION

In the American session, we have the Canadian Retail Sales and the final University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment survey. Canada's retail sales are expected at +0.7% vs +1.2% in the prior month, while the core measure is seen at +0.7% vs +1.2% prior. Good data is unlikely to change much, but bad data could decrease further rate hike expectations amid growth concerns. We recently got soft employment and inflation reports for Canada, yet the market is still pricing in a 62% chance of a BoC hike in December. This is mostly the result of the Bank's hawkish forward guidance, which I consider a mistake.

The final University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment survey is expected at 51.5 vs 51.0 in the preliminary report. The final data is never a market-moving release as traders focus more on preliminary estimates. The recent improvement was driven by falling gasoline prices. However, Director Joanne Hsu noted that while sentiment lifted for lower- and middle-wealth consumers, it fell 5% for those with the largest stock portfolios in the wake of a relatively turbulent period in stock markets. Moreover, consumers’ comments revealed growing anxiety over a possible AI bubble.

item.title: UK October retail sales +0.7% vs +0.0% m/m expected
item.description:
• Prior -0.4% (revised to -0.6%)
  • Retail sales +2.3% vs +1.7% y/y expected
  • Prior +0.8% (revised to +0.4%)
  • Retail sales ex autos, fuel +0.9% vs -0.1% m/m expected
  • Prior -0.7% (revised to -0.9%)
  • Retail sales ex autos, fuel +2.5% vs +1.8% y/y expected
  • Prior +0.8% (revised to +0.4%)
  • Full report

Retail sales rebounded more strongly than expected in October, pointing to improved consumer spending momentum heading into the final quarter of 2026. Retail sales volumes rose by 0.7% m/m, comfortably beating market expectations of no growth, following a downwardly revised 0.6% decline in September. On an annual basis, sales increased by 2.3%, accelerating from a revised 0.4% in September and surpassing expectations of 1.7%.

The underlying figures were equally encouraging. Retail sales excluding autos and fuel rose by 0.9% m/m, against expectations of a 0.1% decline. The annual rate accelerated to 2.5%, up from a revised 0.4% in September.

The October rebound was relatively broad-based. Non-food store sales volumes increased by 1.1% on the month, supported by stronger activity across clothing, art galleries, sports equipment, games and toy stores. Online clothing retailers also reported improved sales as colder, more seasonal weather encouraged consumers to purchase autumn and winter ranges.

Food stores recorded higher sales volumes, partly reflecting increased supermarket purchases of long-life products such as tinned goods and UHT milk following the government's launch of its Be Ready campaign on October 22. Meanwhile, automotive fuel sales volumes fell back to August levels as prices increased for the third consecutive month.

Looking at the broader picture, retail sales volumes increased by 0.4% over the three months to October compared with the previous three-month period. This suggests that the monthly rebound was not entirely isolated, although the underlying recovery in consumer demand remains relatively modest.

Online spending also continued to expand. Online sales values increased by 1.5% m/m and were 9.7% higher than a year earlier. The proportion of total retail sales conducted online edged up to 29.2%, from 29.1% in September.

The data doesn't change much for the Bank of England as the central bank is already expected to hike the Bank Rate by 25 bps at the next meeting in December.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

Asia’s AI trade unravelled on Friday as a sharp reversal on Wall Street spilled into the region’s chipmakers, sending Japanese and South Korean stocks to their steepest losses in weeks. Gold extended its slide to a fresh low for the move. The yen and Japanese government bonds firmed as risk appetite faded heading into a three-day weekend in Japan.

Equities

The Nikkei 225 fell around 4.7%, or roughly 2,820 points, to near 56,620, while the broader TOPIX lost about 3.5%. Advantest, SoftBank Group and Kioxia led the declines. South Korea’s KOSPI dropped about 5.1% and the KOSDAQ nearly 4.9%, with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix each down more than 6%. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell about 2.1% and the Shanghai Composite about 1.6%.

The selling followed a session in which the Nasdaq Composite swung from a gain of more than 2% to a loss of more than 2%, as Anthropic’s record listing failed to lift technology shares. US equity futures stayed soft, with Nasdaq 100 futures down about 0.7% and S&P 500 futures around 0.3% lower. Tokyo markets are closed on Monday for a public holiday.

The China angle sharpened overnight. AMD closed about 8% lower after short seller Hunterbrook, which is short the stock, alleged that a blacklisted Chinese server maker kept using newer AMD firmware, a claim AMD rejects. Separately, a US House committee said Washington approved about 880,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chip shipments to Chinese firms over six months.

Strategists are split on what comes next. UBS downgraded global equities to Neutral in its 2027 outlook, citing concentration and AI risks, days after Morgan Stanley moved to maximum overweight.

The index excluding fresh food and energy slowed to 2.2% from 2.4%. A December hike to 1.50% remains the base case. Some analysts now see rates reaching 2.5% by mid-2027, though markets price an endpoint of around 1.75% to 2%. A Reuters analysis warned the board’s split over the destination could tempt yen bears. JGB yields eased, with the 10-year down about 4 basis points to around 2.80%. USD/JPY slipped to around 159.20.

Morgan joined Deutsche Bank and Bank of America in forecasting hikes in December, January and March, while Barclays expects two. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee warned the AI investment boom risks overheating the economy. The US 10-year Treasury yield held near 5.0%. Posts claiming a $1.756 billion Fed liquidity injection referred to a routine bill purchase held on Wednesday, which adds no net liquidity.

Gold and metals

Spot gold fell about 2.6% to around $3,530 an ounce, extending its slide as Fed hike expectations and high yields weigh. Silver lost more than 3% to around $41.50. UBS upgraded gold to Attractive and sees $5,000 by December 2027, though it has pushed back the timing of that target.

Oil

Brent rose about 0.5% to around $92.40 and WTI was near $82.90. The IEA’s World Energy Outlook called the Hormuz disruption the largest energy supply shock on record, and Executive Director Fatih Birol said there is no credible path back to pre-war markets. Goldman Sachs still sees Brent easing to $78 by end-2027 as bypass pipelines and a supply surplus build.

China

The People’s Bank of China held its one-year and five-year loan prime rates at 3.0% and 3.5% for an 18th month, as expected. The decision carries less weight than it once did, with the central bank’s overnight reverse repo rate now its main policy signal.

FX and crypto

The euro traded near $1.0980, just below the $1.10 level it broke this week on French political risk. Morgan Stanley, Deutsche Bank and another major European lender see $1.08 next year. The Australian dollar was near 0.6660 and the New Zealand dollar near 0.5490. Bitcoin fell about 3% to around $61,600.

The Wall Street Journal reported that US envoys have floated NATO membership for Ukraine in exchange for ceding territory in the Donbas, an idea Moscow rejects. RBA Monetary Policy Board member Renée Fry-McKibbin offered no steer on rates, citing mixed domestic demand, a global oil supply shock and close monitoring of AI.

item.title: Paulson tells Q&A the Fed has more tightening to do, after a speech with no rate steer
item.description:
Paulson’s comments confirm the hawkish lean that her prepared remarks left unsaid, which supports quarter-point December pricing and the view that hikes continue into 2027. Her emphasis on a deliberate pace argues against Waller’s 50 basis point idea, so the comments are more likely to firm up 2027 pricing than lift odds of a jumbo move. That combination supports front-end Treasury yields and the dollar. It’s another headwind for gold, which is already being sold toward $3,600.

--- Paulson’s speech offered no rate steer, but her answers to questions did: more hikes are coming, steadily rather than in a rush.

ps. I meant to post this earlier but it gobbled by tech gremlins and here it is now. 

Summary:

  • Philadelphia Fed President Paulson said in a Q&A that the Fed has more tightening to do
  • She said a deliberate pace of hikes gives the economy time to adjust
  • She described inflation as too high and the job market as at full employment
  • Lowering inflation is the main priority right now, she said
  • Her prepared speech earlier in the evening offered no near-term rate guidance
  • Markets widely expect a quarter-point hike to 4.00% to 4.25% at the December 8 to 9 meeting

Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said the Fed has “more tightening to do,” using a question-and-answer session in New York to fill in what her prepared speech had left out.

Her speech to the Money Marketeers of New York University focused on how the Fed communicates and offered no comment on the near-term rate outlook. When questions turned to policy, she was more direct. In her view, moving at a deliberate pace of hikes gives the economy time to adjust. She described inflation as too high and the job market as at full employment, and said lowering inflation is the main priority right now.

That combination matters. With the labour market at full employment, Paulson sees little reason to hold back on the inflation fight, and her remarks suggest she sees no case for stopping soon. At the same time, her stress on a deliberate pace points to quarter-point steps rather than the half-point December move that Governor Christopher Waller has argued officials should consider.

The comments are consistent with her speech on November 10, when she said policy needs to be somewhat restrictive and that further gradual hikes seemed appropriate. In that speech, she named three developments that would make her favour moving faster: inflation expectations drifting higher, building wage pressures or rising underlying inflation. Earlier on Thursday, she also argued that October’s pause was not mistaken for the end of tightening, and her latest remarks reinforce that point.

Paulson votes on policy this year, and her view lines up with the bulk of the committee. Minutes of the October meeting showed nearly all participants expected further hikes to be appropriate in the coming months. Markets widely expect a quarter-point increase at the December 8 to 9 meeting, which would lift the target range to 4.00% to 4.25%. Several major banks, including J.P. Morgan, Deutsche Bank and Bank of America, expect further moves in January and March.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: UBS cuts global stocks to Neutral, days after Morgan Stanley went maximum overweight
item.description:
The split between two tier-one houses underlines how finely balanced the 2027 equity case is. Concentration in AI-linked megacaps is the fault line. UBS’s preference for the Eurozone, equal-weight US strategies, industrials and health care points to rotation rather than outright selling, which could cushion broader indices even if tech leaders struggle. Higher-for-longer Fed rates and yields above 5% remain the key risk to valuations, so the December 9 Fed decision and the rate path into 2027 matter for both views. For Asia, where AI and chip stocks dominate several indices, UBS’s concentration warning is particularly relevant after Thursday's, now Friday’s, selloff.

---

UBS and Morgan Stanley are looking at the same earnings and the same AI boom, and reaching opposite conclusions about how much risk to take in 2027.

Summary:

  • UBS downgraded global equities to Neutral from Attractive in its Year Ahead 2027 outlook
  • It keeps a constructive earnings view, but says elevated expectations, concentration and AI uncertainty leave less room for disappointment
  • The top 10 S&P 500 stocks, mostly AI-exposed, make up 39% of the index
  • UBS ranks bonds and commodities first, then equities, with cash least preferred
  • It prefers Eurozone stocks, forecasting 15% earnings growth in 2027, and favours industrials, health care and equal-weight US strategies
  • Morgan Stanley moved to maximum overweight days earlier, with an 8,700 S&P 500 target

UBS has downgraded global equities to Neutral from Attractive in its Year Ahead 2027 outlook, arguing that after a multi-year bull run the balance of risk and reward has evened out. The call puts it at odds with Morgan Stanley, which moved global stocks to maximum overweight days earlier.

UBS is not turning bearish on earnings. It says its profit forecasts remain constructive, with global growth near trend and demand for computing capacity supporting AI investment. The problem is what is already priced in. Elevated expectations, heavy index concentration and uncertainty over the AI investment cycle leave less room for disappointment, the bank says. The 10 largest companies in the S&P 500, most of them exposed to AI, now make up 39% of the index. UBS also flags the risk of stickier inflation, higher Federal Reserve rates and higher bond yields, and says markets may start to apply a lower multiple to future earnings as those risks rise.

Across asset classes, UBS now sees the most favourable risk-reward in bonds and commodities, followed by equities, with cash its least preferred holding. Within fixed income, it sees the best opportunities in emerging market and high-yield bonds.

Its central message is to refocus rather than retreat. UBS recommends diversifying away from concentrated technology positions. The Eurozone is its preferred equity market, where it forecasts earnings growth of 15% in 2027, comparable with the S&P 500 but from a lower starting valuation and with a broader range of drivers. At the sector level it favours industrials and health care, and it suggests equal-weight strategies in the US to reduce exposure to the biggest technology names. The equal-weighted S&P 500 has outperformed the standard market-cap-weighted index by about 7 percentage points since the start of June.

The contrast with Morgan Stanley is sharp. That bank’s 2027 outlook argues risk assets have cheapened enough to justify taking more risk, and sets an S&P 500 target of 8,700, about 15% above recent levels. Barclays and Goldman Sachs also see 8,700. UBS reads the same backdrop of solid earnings and continued AI spending, but concludes that concentration and valuation risks argue for a more cautious, broader stance.

The debate is playing out in real time. On Thursday the Nasdaq swung from a gain of more than 2% to a loss of more than 2%, and on Friday Japan’s Nikkei fell as much as 4.5% as AI and semiconductor stocks were sold across Asia. Days like these make UBS’s case for diversification look timely, though a single session settles little about a full-year call.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: No, the Fed isn’t pumping $1.756 billion into markets on Friday morning: what that viral post gets wrong
item.description:
These operations are pre-announced, small relative to the Treasury market and reserve-neutral, so they carry no policy signal. The real liquidity story is the Fed’s hiking path (eg. J.P. Morgan now sees three straight Fed hikes, dropping its ‘December and done’ call ) and year-end funding conditions, where rising net bill supply, not these purchases, is the main influence on reserves. Traders watching for genuine balance sheet signals should focus on any change in the Desk’s language about reserve conditions, or a return of reserve management purchases.

---

The Fed’s “liquidity injection” is just its monthly bill reinvestment schedule doing what it always does, and the operation in question has already happened.

Summary:

  • Social media posts claim the Fed is set to inject $1.756 billion of liquidity around the US market open
  • The figure matches a New York Fed Treasury bill purchase held on November 18, scheduled in advance
  • The Desk plans about $14 billion of reinvestment purchases from November 16 to December 11, and no reserve management purchases
  • Reinvestment purchases replace maturing holdings and do not expand the balance sheet or add net reserves
  • There is no operation scheduled for Friday, and the next is on November 24
  • The Fed remains on a hiking path, with a December 9 rate rise widely expected

Posts circulating on social media claim the Federal Reserve is set to inject $1.756 billion of liquidity into the financial system around the US market open to support a volatile Wall Street. The claim is misleading. The figure matches a routine Treasury bill purchase by the New York Fed, scheduled weeks in advance, which took place on Wednesday and adds no net liquidity.

You can check for yourself: Treasury Securities Operational Details - FEDERAL RESERVE BANK of NEW YORK

-

The New York Fed’s trading desk publishes a monthly schedule of these operations. For the period from November 16 to December 11, it plans about $14 billion of what it calls reinvestment purchases, with no reserve management purchases. The schedule lists five operations, each running from 9:00 to 9:20 am US Eastern time. The $1.756 billion operation, for bills maturing in four to 12 months, was held on November 18. The next is set for November 24, for up to about $3.5 billion, and a second $1.756 billion purchase is scheduled for December 3. There is no operation on Friday.

The type of purchase matters. Reinvestment purchases replace securities in the Fed’s portfolio as older holdings, mainly agency mortgage-backed securities and agency debt, pay down. The Fed is swapping one asset for another, so its balance sheet does not grow and no net new reserves are created. That is different from reserve management purchases, which do expand the balance sheet, and which the Fed is not conducting this month.

The timing is also routine. These operations run in the same early-morning slot whatever the market backdrop, and the amounts follow a fixed pattern set out in advance, not a response to this week’s volatility.

The bigger picture runs the other way. The Fed is in a hiking cycle, with markets widely expecting a quarter-point increase on December 9. Readers can check any future claims against the New York Fed’s published schedule and results pages, which show the planned and actual size of each operation.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: A December BoJ hike may not be enough: why a fuzzy endpoint keeps yen bears circling
item.description:
With a December hike largely priced, the yen’s direction now hinges on the BoJ’s guidance beyond it. A vague statement or a cautious press conference from Ueda on December 18 risks a “hike and sell” reaction like last December’s. A clearer commitment to keep tightening toward 2% would give the yen more durable support. Until then, intervention risk near 160 is doing more to cap USD/JPY than rate expectations are. The July board changes add a longer-dated dovish tail risk that could weigh on yen forwards.

--- The BoJ is agreed on December but divided on the destination, and that missing endpoint may matter more to the yen than the hike itself.

Summary:

  • Most BoJ policymakers back a December hike to 1.50%, but the board is split on how far rates should ultimately rise
  • BoJ staff estimate the neutral rate at between 1.1% and 2.5%, with no board consensus on where it sits
  • Markets and economists see the cycle ending at around 1.75% to 2%
  • The yen fell after last December’s hike as markets judged the message unconvincing
  • Hawks Tamura and Takata leave the board in July, giving PM Takaichi two appointments
  • USD/JPY held above the mid-159s after Friday’s inflation data

A Bank of Japan rate hike in December looks all but settled, but that may not be enough to steady the yen. A Reuters analysis argues that the board’s lack of agreement on how far rates should eventually rise could give currency bears a fresh opening, even as the bank keeps tightening.

The near-term case for a hike strengthened this week. Governor Kazuo Ueda told parliament on Thursday that recent soft consumption was temporary, and October inflation data released on Friday showed core prices above the 2% target for a second month. Most economists expect a move to 1.50% at the December 17 to 18 meeting, followed by another by the end of March.

The problem is the destination. BoJ staff estimate Japan’s nominal neutral rate, the level that neither stimulates nor restrains the economy, at anywhere between 1.1% and 2.5%. The board has not agreed where in that range it sits. Hawk Naoki Tamura puts it at about 2%. Hajime Takata favours lifting rates to a level near the middle of the range while avoiding fixed hiking intervals. Doves Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato see more limited room to tighten. Markets regard Junko Koeda and Kazuyuki Masu as the swing votes on timing.

That uncertainty matters for the yen because it caps how far traders are willing to price. Markets and economists polled by Reuters see the cycle ending at roughly 1.75% to 2%, well short of the most aggressive outside calls. Some analysts this week said rates could reach 2.5% by mid-2027, but that view remains an outlier. Nomura’s Mari Iwashita said the BoJ may be avoiding clear guidance because anchoring inflation around 2% is new territory. In her view, though, sustained US rate hikes would keep pressure on it to keep raising rates.

History offers a warning. In December last year, the yen fell even though the BoJ raised rates, as markets judged the hawkish message unconvincing. The same risk applies now, with the Federal Reserve also hiking and keeping the US-Japan rate gap wide.

Politics adds another layer. Two hawks, Tamura and Takata, leave the nine-member board when their terms expire in July, giving Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi the chance to appoint replacements. Analysts say one seat may go to a less hawkish candidate. Takaichi has said little about rate policy. One veteran BoJ watcher questioned whether she would take steps that weaken the yen, which he sees as the key influence on how far the bank goes.

USD/JPY dropped toward 159.00 on Friday. For the yen, December’s hike looks priced. What the BoJ signals about the path beyond it will matter more.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: No way back for oil after Hormuz, says IEA’s Birol, but Goldman still sees Brent at $78
item.description:
For oil, the two views point to a split between the structure of the market and the price. Long-dated risk premiums tied to Hormuz may persist as importers pay up for security of supply. Near-dated Brent faces pressure from a growing surplus and new bypass capacity. Brent’s muted reaction to fresh mine claims supports Goldman’s view that the market is becoming less sensitive to headlines from the strait. Diesel and jet fuel remain the tightest part of the complex, so refining margins could stay elevated even if crude eases. Importers in Asia carry the most exposure, given their heavy reliance on Gulf supply.

---

The IEA says the Hormuz crisis has changed energy markets for good, while Goldman says the adjustment is already happening fast enough to pull oil prices lower.

Summary:

  • IEA head Fatih Birol says there is no credible path back to pre-war energy markets, as confidence in Hormuz has been crushed
  • The IEA’s World Energy Outlook 2026 calls the disruption the largest energy supply shock on record, with 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 bcm of gas lost from the Gulf
  • At its peak, global oil supply fell by 16 mb/d and gas supply by 320 million cubic metres per day
  • The IEA says bypass routes and demand measures could cut reliance on the strait from 20 mb/d to 8.5 mb/d by 2030 and below 2 mb/d by 2035
  • Goldman Sachs expects 3.8 mb/d of new bypass pipeline capacity over the next year and a 2 mb/d oil surplus in 2027
  • Goldman sees Brent averaging $88 in 2027 and easing to $78 by December

The International Energy Agency says energy markets will not return to where they were before the Iran war, even if the world can learn to manage without the Strait of Hormuz. “I don’t see any credible pathway back” to the pre-war situation, IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol wrote in an article for The Economist, arguing that confidence in the strait as a safe and reliable corridor has been crushed.

His comments accompany the IEA’s World Energy Outlook 2026, released on Thursday. It describes the Hormuz disruption as the largest energy supply shock the world has faced, and one that is not yet over. At its peak, global oil supply fell by 16 million barrels per day and gas supply by 320 million cubic metres per day. By November, cumulative losses from the Gulf had reached 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres of gas, far larger than any previous crisis.

The system has absorbed more than many expected. Well-stocked inventories, the IEA’s largest co-ordinated stock release, bypass routes for some Gulf exports, higher Atlantic basin supply and a sharp drop in Chinese crude imports all cushioned the blow. But the IEA says the burden is increasingly shifting to consumers through high prices and demand destruction, with diesel and jet fuel hit hardest. It estimates global spending on imported oil and gas will reach $1.6 trillion this year, a quarter more than in 2025.

The lasting change, in Birol’s view, is diversification. Countries will seek a wider mix of fuels, technologies, suppliers and trade routes. That includes pipelines that carry Middle East oil around Hormuz, which he says the UAE and Saudi Arabia are already building quickly. The IEA estimates that bypass pipelines, alternative supplies and demand measures could cut the need for oil flows through the strait from 20 million barrels per day before the crisis to 8.5 million by 2030, and below 2 million by 2035. Even then, it says, the Middle East would remain the world’s largest oil exporter.

Goldman Sachs sees that adaptation already weighing on prices. The bank expects about 3.8 million barrels per day of new bypass pipeline capacity over the next year, sending crude to the Gulf of Oman, the Red Sea or the Mediterranean. It estimates the oil market tipped into surplus in October, as Gulf exports recovered to their 2025 average, and expects that surplus to reach 2 million barrels per day in 2027. Its forecast has Brent averaging $88 next year and easing toward $78 by December 2027.

Markets are already showing signs of that shift, barely moving despite Iranian claims that two supertankers had struck mines in the strait. The two views can both prove right: the energy system may be permanently changed, even as the price premium from the crisis gradually fades. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US envoys float NATO membership for Ukraine in exchange for Donbas, WSJ reports
item.description:
The report shows active diplomacy but no convergence, so markets are unlikely to price a settlement soon. European defence stocks are the most headline-sensitive, and any sign of a breakthrough would test their rally. A credible peace path would eventually weigh on European gas prices and diesel cracks, where Russian refining and product exports have been a supply risk, and could support the euro. For oil, the Middle East remains the bigger driver, so Ukraine headlines are a secondary factor for crude itself.

---

Washington has put Ukraine’s NATO membership on the table as a bargaining chip, but Moscow wants the opposite and Berlin isn’t on board, so a deal still looks distant.

Summary:

  • US envoys have discussed NATO membership for Ukraine in exchange for ceding territory, according to The Wall Street Journal
  • One US scenario trades Ukraine’s remaining Donbas territory for full membership, and another freezes the front line with treaty-based security guarantees
  • Zelensky confirmed the question was raised but says Ukraine will not give up its land
  • Russia’s non-paper demands Ukraine drop its NATO aspirations, and seeks a NATO rollback in Eastern Europe to 1997 levels
  • France supports discussing membership while Germany is opposed, and NATO expands only by consensus
  • A US official says many ideas are being discussed and both sides must agree

US envoys have floated the idea of NATO membership for Ukraine in exchange for Kyiv ceding territory to Russia, a proposal that would break with long-standing US policy and run directly against Moscow’s demands, The Wall Street Journal (gated) reported.

According to people familiar with the talks cited by the Journal, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have raised the idea in several conversations with European officials in recent months. Most recently it came up with President Volodymyr Zelensky and European national security advisers at a meeting in Dublin last week. It was also raised in at least one meeting in the United Arab Emirates involving Ukrainian, European and Russian negotiators.

The US has put two scenarios on the table, the report said. The first would see Ukraine give up the part of the Donbas region it still controls in return for full NATO membership. The second would freeze the conflict along the current front line, leaving some of the Donbas in Ukrainian hands, with security guarantees provided through a treaty with the US and possibly European allies. A US official said many ideas are under discussion and that both Ukraine and Russia would have to agree to any final deal.

It is unclear how seriously the idea is being pursued, or whether President Donald Trump has changed his view. He ruled out Ukrainian NATO membership early last year as unacceptable to Russia. Zelensky confirmed the question had been raised, recounting that the Americans asked, “What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?” He has said repeatedly that Ukraine will not give up its land, and that any deal would need approval from the Ukrainian people.

Moscow’s position points the other way. In a non-paper seen by the Journal, Russian negotiators demanded that Ukraine remove its NATO aspirations from its constitution, that the alliance commit not to station troops or equipment in Ukraine, and that Western arms deliveries stop. They also called for NATO to roll back military infrastructure in Eastern Europe to 1997 levels. European negotiators described the demands as maximalist opening bids.

Divisions within NATO add a further hurdle, since the alliance can only expand by consensus. French President Emmanuel Macron said after talks in Berlin on Thursday that it was time to discuss Ukraine’s membership. German officials were unwilling to pursue it, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz has told aides he does not expect Ukraine to join in his lifetime. Kushner said separately that Russia had become comfortable with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine.

For markets, the report is a reminder that peace talks are active but far from a deal. Any credible move toward a settlement would be watched closely in European defence stocks, European gas prices and the euro, and in oil product markets, where Russian refining and export flows have been a source of supply risk. With Russia and Ukraine still far apart on core issues, those markets are likely to treat individual headlines with caution. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ICYMI: AMD slides 8% as short seller Hunterbrook ties its firmware to a blacklisted Chinese firm
item.description:
The allegations add a legal and regulatory overhang to a stock already hit by tighter US export licensing this month. Commerce’s response, or silence, is now the key variable. The China and Singapore revenue figures give bears a concrete number to point to, which could keep pressure on AMD even without any enforcement action. For the wider sector, a second short-seller campaign on China ties raises the risk premium on US chipmakers with large Asian sales, adding to the selling already hitting Asian chip stocks. Any sign of a BIS inquiry would be a fresh catalyst.

---

Earlier:

  • US approved nearly 900,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chips for China. Raises more questions than answers.

--- A short seller has put AMD’s China exposure in the spotlight, but by its own admission it hasn’t shown that any law was broken.

Summary:

  • AMD shares fell as much as 11% on Thursday and closed about 8% lower after Hunterbrook published a short report
  • Hunterbrook alleges IEIT Systems, blacklisted in March 2025, built at least six newer versions of AMD firmware into server updates
  • It says it cannot establish how IEIT obtained the code, whether a licence existed or that any export violation occurred
  • Hunterbrook’s investment arm is short AMD
  • AMD says the claims misrepresent its business and that it complies with US export laws
  • Hunterbrook says China and Hong Kong accounted for about 22% of AMD’s fiscal 2025 revenue

AMD shares fell as much as 11% on Thursday and closed about 8% lower after short seller Hunterbrook published a report alleging that a Chinese server maker on a US government blacklist has continued to use newer versions of the chipmaker’s software. Hunterbrook’s investment arm disclosed a short position in AMD, meaning it profits if the shares fall.

The report, titled “AMD has its own China problem,” centres on IEIT Systems, an arm of China’s Inspur Group. The Commerce Department added IEIT to its Entity List in March 2025 over its role in China’s supercomputer programme. Hunterbrook says IEIT has since built at least six newer versions of AMD’s startup firmware into server updates. The most recent was an update dated October 19, 2026, which contained firmware AMD released in July. It also says firmware posted by three other server companies, including Aivres, is nearly identical to IEIT’s, and points to corporate links between them.

Hunterbrook argues that software updates can count as exports under US rules, citing a recent enforcement settlement in which each post-listing update was treated as a separate violation. But it is careful about what it cannot show. It says it does not know how IEIT obtained the code or whether anyone held a licence, and that its findings do not establish an export violation. The Commerce Department has not commented.

AMD rejected the report. “The claims misrepresent AMD’s business practices and relationships,” a spokesperson said. The company added that it complies with US export control laws, maintains rigorous compliance processes across its global operations and remains focused on its customers.

For investors, the bigger question is China exposure. Citing AMD’s filings, Hunterbrook says billings to customers in China and Hong Kong were about $7.8 billion in fiscal 2025, roughly 22% of total revenue of about $35 billion, with a further $4.3 billion billed to Singapore. Singapore is among the countries covered by a new US licensing rule aimed at stopping advanced chips from reaching China through third countries. Hunterbrook also argues that AMD’s plan to grow data center AI revenue by more than 80% a year rests on the very chips facing tighter restrictions.

The report lands in a difficult month for US chipmakers. AMD had already fallen sharply in mid-November as Washington tightened export licensing, and Nvidia is facing its own short-seller scrutiny over China ties. With US lawmakers also releasing data this week on AI chip approvals for Chinese firms, the political pressure for stricter controls shows little sign of easing.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Some analysts now see BoJ rates at 2.5% by mid-2027, despite slower underlying inflation
item.description:
A 2.5% BoJ path is far from priced, so the forecast is more a marker of upside risk than a market mover. If the coming months show underlying inflation turning higher, front-end JGB yields would be the first to reprice, with the yen likely to follow. The view also raises the stakes for the BoJ’s December 18 statement and Ueda’s press conference, where any hint of a faster pace would carry weight. With energy and imported costs feeding producer prices, oil and USD/JPY remain the key inputs to watch.

---

October’s slower underlying inflation hasn’t deterred the BoJ hawks: some forecasters now see rates at 2.5% by mid-2027, double today’s level.

Summary:

  • Some analysts expect a sharp acceleration in Japan’s inflation excluding fresh food and energy, despite October’s slowdown to 2.2% from 2.4%
  • They see further room for goods inflation and say producer prices point to faster food price rises
  • Some now expect the BoJ policy rate to reach 2.5% by mid-2027, up from earlier calls of around 2%
  • That would take five quarter-point hikes from today’s 1.25%, far faster than consensus
  • A Reuters poll shows 86% expect a hike to 1.50% in December and nearly 60% see 1.75% by end-March
  • Fresh food and briefly reduced utility subsidies lifted October’s headline reading to 2.3%

Some analysts are making a far more aggressive case for Bank of Japan tightening than the market, arguing that October’s slower underlying inflation reading is a pause rather than a turning point.

Japan’s core-core index, which excludes fresh food and energy and is closely watched by the BoJ, slowed to 2.2% in October from 2.4%. One camp of forecasters argues that a sharp acceleration in that measure is still likely over the coming months. They see further room for inflation in other industrial products, a broad category of manufactured goods, and say producer price data point to faster food inflation ahead. October’s producer prices rose 7.1% year on year, beating forecasts. Oil, chemicals, steel and utility costs climbed, and a weak yen pushed up import costs. Companies are still passing those costs on to consumers.

On that basis, some analysts now expect the BoJ to raise its policy rate to 2.5% by the middle of 2027. That marks a big step up from the same camp’s call only a month ago for a peak of around 2%, which was itself seen as above consensus. The pace is the sticking point. The BoJ has settled into a roughly quarterly rhythm of quarter-point hikes, moving in June and September and widely expected to act again in December. At that pace, the policy rate would reach about 2% by mid-2027. Getting to 2.5% from today’s 1.25% would require a hike at every one of the five meetings between December and June, or a larger move along the way. That would be a clear break from the steady approach the bank has followed so far.

The mainstream view is more measured. A Reuters poll shows 86% of economists expect a hike to 1.50% at the December 17 to 18 meeting, and nearly 60% expect 1.75% by the end of March. Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Thursday that the bank expects to keep raising rates. He flagged an upside risk that underlying inflation could overshoot the 2% target, but he has given no sign of an accelerated path.

There are also reasons for caution in the October data. Headline inflation rose to 2.3%, its highest in nearly a year. That was driven partly by a sharp increase in fresh food prices and by energy costs after the government briefly scaled back utility subsidies. Those subsidies are expected to return over the winter, which could take some heat out of headline readings in the coming months.

The debate matters for the yen. A BoJ path toward 2.5% would narrow the rate gap with the US far more quickly than markets expect, offering support for a currency trading near 160 per dollar. If underlying inflation instead stays around 2%, the gradual path priced by most economists looks more likely, and the yen would remain reliant on intervention warnings.

item.title: US approved nearly 900,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chips for China. Raises more questions than answers.
item.description:
The disclosure adds to political pressure for tighter China chip rules, a risk for Nvidia and AMD’s China revenue at a time when AI and semiconductor shares are already being sold hard across Asia. Nvidia saying it has stopped H200 shipments limits the near-term earnings hit, but any formal tightening would also weigh on Chinese AI developers’ access to computing power. Hong Kong-listed Tencent, Alibaba and Baidu are the most exposed names on the Chinese side. The story also keeps Washington’s broader export-control push in focus, including reported plans to curb advanced chip exports to parts of Southeast Asia.

---

Washington’s own licensing data show it cleared hundreds of thousands of AI chips for Chinese firms, including military-listed ones, handing China hawks fresh ammunition just as Nvidia says it has stopped shipping.

Summary:

  • The Commerce Department approved about 880,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chip shipments to Chinese firms from December 2025 to May 2026
  • Approvals included 150,000 for Tencent, 75,000 for Alibaba, 43,000 for Baidu and 4,000 for BYD, all on the Pentagon’s military-linked list
  • Companies had sought licences for more than 3.4 million chips
  • It is unclear how many approved chips were actually delivered, and Nvidia says it has stopped shipping H200s to China
  • Commerce says licensing follows a January 2026 rule with extra national security requirements
  • The House committee called the release the most detailed public disclosure under the 2018 Export Control Reform Act

The US Commerce Department approved shipments of about 880,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD to Chinese companies between December 2025 and May 2026, according to licensing data released on Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

The approvals covered Nvidia’s H200 and AMD’s equivalent MI325X. They included 150,000 chips for Tencent, 75,000 for Alibaba, 43,000 for Baidu and 4,000 for BYD. All four companies appear on the Pentagon’s list of alleged Chinese military-backed firms, and together they account for just over 30% of the approved total. Companies had sought permission to ship more than 3.4 million chips over the period, so roughly a quarter of requested volumes were approved.

It is not clear how many of the approvals turned into actual deliveries. Nvidia said the licences came with strict conditions and limited volumes and that “we have since stopped shipping H200s to China.” AMD said it complies with US export control laws. Reuters reported in May that about 10 Chinese companies had been cleared to buy the H200 but no deliveries had been made. A Commerce official later told the committee that shipments had begun but there had been very few.

The Commerce Department said its H200 licensing follows a January 2026 rule that adds significant national security requirements for applicants, allowing case-by-case review rather than a presumption of denial. Critics are unconvinced. A former US official who specialises in US-China technology policy called the share going to military-listed firms astonishing and questioned whether Commerce had carried out a serious security review.

The release is unusual. Committee Chair Brian Mast described it as the most detailed public disclosure since the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 expanded Commerce’s powers over sensitive technology exports. It comes as the Trump administration faces closer scrutiny of its China chip policy following reports involving former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese spy, which have revived calls in Washington for a tougher stance.

The policy backdrop has swung sharply. The Biden administration restricted Chinese access to advanced AI chips over concerns they would strengthen China’s military and erode the US lead in AI. President Trump reversed course in December 2025, allowing Nvidia to ship the H200 to China. With pressure building on both sides of the political divide, investors will watch for any move to tighten licensing again. That would weigh on chipmakers’ China revenue and on Chinese tech firms’ access to advanced computing. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: China holds loan prime rates for an 18th month as the overnight rate takes over
item.description:
A hold was expected, so it should leave the yuan and Chinese bond markets little changed. The five respondents who expected a cut show that easing talk is building, which keeps attention on the PBoC’s next steps outside the LPR, such as reserve requirement cuts or targeted lending. Weak October activity data and a hawkish Fed narrow the room for rate cuts, since a lower rate would widen the gap with the US and add pressure to the yuan. For Asian equities, already under pressure from today’s chip selloff, the decision offers no fresh support.

Newswire cut: China kept its one-year loan prime rate at 3.0% and five-year at 3.5% for an 18th straight month, as expected by most. The LPR still prices most loans and mortgages, but the PBoC’s main signal is now its 1.25% overnight reverse repo rate.

One-line wrap: China’s lending benchmarks held steady again, a reminder that the LPR now follows Beijing’s policy signals rather than setting them.

Summary:

  • China held its one-year LPR at 3.0% and five-year LPR at 3.5%, an 18th consecutive month unchanged
  • 23 of 28 participants in a Reuters survey expected a hold, while five forecast a cut
  • The one-year rate is the benchmark for most corporate and household loans, and the five-year rate anchors mortgages
  • The LPR follows the PBoC’s policy operations rather than signalling policy itself
  • Since November 2, overnight reverse repo operations at 1.25% have been the PBoC’s main daily operation, replacing the seven-day repo
  • The PBoC plans to let strong companies price loans off the overnight rate, further reducing the LPR’s role

China left its benchmark lending rates unchanged for an 18th consecutive month on Friday. The one-year loan prime rate stayed at 3.0% and the five-year rate at 3.5%, in line with expectations from most market participants.

A Reuters survey of 28 respondents had found 23 expecting no change. Five forecast a cut to one or both rates, the first break from unanimous hold calls in recent months. That minority view reflected signs of renewed weakness in October, with factory output slowing and consumption subdued. Citigroup had described a November cut as implausible and expects rates to stay on hold through the rest of 2026, followed by two 10 basis point cuts in 2027.

What the LPR is

The loan prime rate is a benchmark lending rate set once a month. Twenty designated commercial banks submit quotes to the People’s Bank of China, and the published rate is meant to reflect what banks charge their most creditworthy borrowers. Other loans are priced as a spread above it.

What the two rates are used for

The one-year LPR is the reference for most corporate and household loans, including working capital lending to businesses. The five-year LPR is the main benchmark for mortgages, which makes it the rate to watch for any support aimed at the property sector.

Why it matters less than it used to

The LPR is not the PBoC’s policy rate. Banks set their quotes based on the central bank’s own operations, so the LPR tends to follow policy moves rather than signal them. For years, the medium-term lending facility played that anchoring role. In 2024 the PBoC made the seven-day reverse repo rate its main policy rate, most recently at 1.40%.

The bank has now gone a step further. From November 2, overnight reverse repo operations at 1.25% became the PBoC’s main daily operation, with seven-day operations kept as a liquidity tool used as needed. Governor Pan Gongsheng said in October that the interbank overnight repo rate had effectively become the central bank’s target. Analysts stress the switch is a reform rather than a rate cut, even though it lowered the floor of the rate framework by 15 basis points.

The PBoC also plans to let financially strong companies price loans off the overnight rate rather than the LPR. Over time, that would weaken the LPR’s role even in its core job of pricing bank loans.

For markets, that means a monthly LPR hold tells investors little on its own. Any shift in China’s policy stance is now more likely to show up first in the overnight rate, in reserve requirement changes or in targeted lending tools, with the LPR following later.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

Wall Street’s whiplash session hit Asia’s AI darlings hardest, and a three-day weekend in Japan gave Tokyo investors one more reason to sell first.

Summary:

  • The Nikkei fell as much as 4.5%, dropping below 57,000 to a two-week low
  • Topix -2.7%
  • South Korea’s KOSPI fell more than 4% in early trade
  • The Nasdaq Composite swung from a gain of over 2% to a loss of over 2% as AI and chip stocks were sold
  • Anthropic’s record fundraising and Nasdaq debut failed to lift tech, with some investors citing selling in other assets to buy the shares
  • Advantest, SoftBank Group and Kioxia led Tokyo’s declines, and SK Hynix and Samsung each fell more than 5%
  • Japan’s markets are closed on Monday for a holiday, adding to risk aversion

Japanese and South Korean stocks tumbled on Friday as a sharp reversal in US technology shares spilled into Asia, hitting the region’s AI and semiconductor names hardest. Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell as much as 4.5%, dropping below 57,000 to a two-week low, while South Korea’s KOSPI slid more than 4% in early trade.

The selling followed a volatile session on Wall Street. The Nasdaq Composite swung from a gain of more than 2% to a loss of more than 2%, a reversal of over four percentage points in a single day. The move came as Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut after a record-sized fundraising, and the listing failed to lift the wider technology sector. Some investors pointed to selling in other holdings to raise cash for Anthropic shares, a rotation that may have drained money from established AI names.

In Tokyo, chip-testing equipment maker Advantest, SoftBank Group and memory chipmaker Kioxia led the declines. In Seoul, SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics each fell more than 5%. All four have been among the biggest beneficiaries of AI-related spending, which leaves them exposed when sentiment toward the theme turns.

Timing added to the pressure in Japan. Monday is a public holiday, so Tokyo markets are closed for three days, and investors appeared reluctant to hold risk over a long weekend in a market this volatile.

The broader backdrop has been difficult for high-valuation technology stocks. US Treasury yields are holding above 5% as markets price further Federal Reserve hikes, with several major banks now expecting moves in December, January and March. Higher yields reduce the present value of future earnings, which weighs most on growth-oriented sectors such as AI and semiconductors. Questions over the payback on AI investment have also grown, with UBS downgrading global equities to Neutral in its 2027 outlook and flagging concentration and AI execution risks.

For now, the moves look like a sentiment-driven selloff rather than a reaction to any single piece of company news. How US futures trade through the Asian session, and whether the Nasdaq can stabilise on Friday, will set the tone for Seoul and for Tokyo when it reopens on Tuesday.

item.title: Japan CPI misses on all three measures, but core stays above 2% ahead of a BoJ hike call
item.description:
The misses take a little edge off December hike pricing, but not enough to change the base case after Ueda’s hawkish remarks on Thursday. A slower underlying gauge leaves the yen with less support than it needed near 160, so the burden falls on intervention warnings rather than rate expectations. JGB yields may ease at the front end, but producer prices running at 7.1% keep the inflation pipeline full. With energy a key driver, oil remains a swing factor for whether underlying inflation turns back up as some economists expect.

----

The data post earlier:

  • Japan inflation picks up less than forecast as core-core slows to 2.2%

Japan’s inflation missed forecasts across the board but stayed above target, leaving the BoJ’s December hike intact and the yen still looking for support near 160.

Summary:

  • Core CPI (excluding fresh food) rose 2.2% y/y in October, against a 2.3% forecast and 2.1% in September
  • Headline CPI rose to 2.3% from 2.1%, below the 2.5% forecast
  • The index excluding fresh food and fuel slowed to 2.2% from 2.4%, against a 2.3% forecast
  • Core inflation has exceeded the BoJ’s 2% target for a second straight month
  • 86% of economists polled expect a hike to 1.50% at the December 17 to 18 meeting, and one research house sees 2.5% by mid-2027
  • The BoJ’s policy rate is 1.25% after hikes in June and September

Japan’s core inflation rate picked up in October and stayed above the Bank of Japan’s 2% target for a second straight month, although every major measure came in below forecasts. The result does little to change expectations that the BoJ will raise rates at its December meeting.

The core consumer price index, which excludes fresh food, rose 2.2% from a year earlier, below the median forecast of 2.3% but up from 2.1% in September. Headline inflation rose to 2.3% from 2.1%, short of the 2.5% expected. The index that excludes both fresh food and fuel, which the BoJ watches as a better gauge of demand-driven price pressure, slowed to 2.2% from 2.4%, against a forecast of 2.3%.

That last reading is the one that gives doves something to point to. A slowdown in underlying inflation would normally argue for patience. But the gauge is still above target, and some economists expect it to accelerate sharply in the coming months as companies continue to pass on rising raw material costs. One research house now expects the BoJ to lift its policy rate to 2.5% by the middle of next year, well beyond current market pricing.

Cost pressures in the pipeline support that view. Japan’s producer prices rose 7.1% year on year in October, ahead of forecasts. Oil, chemicals, steel and utilities drove the rise, and a weak yen lifted import costs. Energy costs tied to the Middle East conflict have been a major driver of the pickup in consumer prices this year.

The BoJ’s policy rate stands at 1.25% after hikes in June and September, a faster pace than its roughly twice-yearly moves in 2024 and 2025. It held rates steady in October. A Reuters poll shows 86% of economists expect a hike to 1.50% at the December 17 to 18 meeting, which would be the third increase this year. Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Thursday that the bank expects to keep raising rates because monetary conditions remain accommodative. He also flagged an upside risk that underlying inflation could overshoot the target.

There are offsetting concerns. The economy unexpectedly contracted in the July to September quarter, and the yen is trading near 160 per dollar despite heavy intervention this year. With the Fed also hiking, a December BoJ move may do little to narrow the rate gap that has kept pressure on the yen.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6731 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold slides toward $3,600 as sellers press on, but UBS upgrades it and still sees $5,000
item.description:
UBS’s upgrade gives longer-term buyers a reason to look at gold at these levels. But the near-term flow still belongs to rates, and nothing in the call changes the picture before the December 9 Fed decision. The low $3,600s are now being tested, and a clean break would leave the market with little obvious support until the high $3,500s. A short-covering bounce is possible if US data soften or the dollar pauses, but rallies are likely to meet selling while three-hike forecasts keep spreading.

---

Earlier:

  • Gold at $3,625: five forces behind the sell-off, and four reasons buyers haven’t quit

---

Gold keeps falling on Fed hike bets, while UBS says the wait for a recovery is getting longer but the case for owning it at these prices is getting stronger.

Summary:

  • Gold has slipped to around $3,606, roughly 35% below January’s record, as hawkish Fed expectations, 5% Treasury yields and a firm dollar weigh
  • UBS has upgraded gold to Attractive in its Year Ahead 2027 outlook, forecasting $5,000 an ounce by December 2027
  • It cites structural demand and an eventual easing in real yields, with bond yields seen declining modestly later in 2027
  • The bank ranks bonds and commodities above equities, which it downgraded to Neutral, with cash least preferred
  • UBS’s $5,000 target has slipped from the first half of 2027 to the fourth quarter as the Fed turned more hawkish
  • It sees oil supported in the first half and names copper its preferred industrial metal

Gold is under heavy selling pressure again, slipping to around $3,606 an ounce in Asian trade and extending a slide that has taken it roughly 35% below its January record. The pressure is coming from the same place as all year: expectations that the Federal Reserve will keep raising rates. J.P. Morgan became the latest major bank on Thursday to forecast hikes in December, January and March. Treasury yields above 5% and a firm dollar continue to raise the cost of holding a metal that pays no income.

Against that backdrop, UBS has moved the other way. In its Year Ahead 2027 outlook, titled “Sustaining resilience,” the bank has upgraded gold to Attractive. It argues that structural demand and an eventual easing in real yields should support a recovery toward $5,000 an ounce by December 2027, which would be a gain of close to 40% from current levels.

The upgrade is part of a broader shift in UBS’s asset allocation. The bank now sees the most favourable risk-reward in bonds and commodities, followed by equities, with cash its least preferred asset class, and it has downgraded global equities to Neutral. It describes commodities as a way to protect portfolios against geopolitical disruption, inflation and constrained supply, with gold at the centre of that view.

UBS’s path to $5,000 has lengthened as the Fed has turned more hawkish. In August, the bank expected gold to reach $5,000 in the first half of 2027. As recently as October, its chief investment office saw $5,400 by September 2027. Earlier this week it pushed the $5,000 level back to the final quarter of 2027. The new outlook keeps that target but adds conviction through the upgrade. In effect, UBS is arguing that the wait may be longer, but the case is stronger at today’s prices.

The key condition is real yields. UBS expects easing inflation to allow bond yields to decline modestly later in 2027, and its chief investment office has forecast Fed hikes in December and March before that relief arrives. That sequencing explains the gap between the price and the forecast. Until real yields turn, the structural buyers UBS is counting on, chiefly central banks, are more likely to slow gold’s decline than reverse it.

Elsewhere in commodities, UBS expects oil to remain supported in the first half of 2027 and names copper as its preferred industrial metal, citing demand from electrification, power networks, data centres and AI infrastructure.

The call puts UBS among the more constructive major banks on gold, alongside Morgan Stanley at $5,250 for the fourth quarter of 2027 and ahead of Goldman Sachs at $4,650 for the end of next year. All three see higher prices from here. None sees a quick turn while the Fed is still hiking. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed's Paulson keeps quiet on December, says October’s pause was never meant as a stop
item.description:
With no fresh policy signal, the speech is unlikely to move rate pricing, and a quarter-point December hike remains the strong favourite. Her “pause was not a stop” framing supports the view that the hiking cycle runs into 2027, which keeps front-end Treasury yields and the dollar supported. Her three triggers for faster hikes give traders a checklist for the 4 December payrolls report and other data before the meeting: inflation expectations, wage growth and underlying inflation. An upside surprise on wages or expectations would strengthen the case for the larger move that Waller has floated.

---

Earlier:

  • JPMorgan now sees three straight Fed hikes, dropping its ‘December and done’ call

---

Paulson argues the Fed should need to say less if markets understand it, and her policy view hasn’t changed: gradual hikes, with three clear reasons to go faster.

Summary:

  • Philadelphia Fed President Paulson offered no comment on the near-term rate outlook in a speech in New York
  • She said shared understanding of the Fed’s reaction function matters more than explicit forward guidance, which she said is less valuable in normal times
  • She said October’s hold after the September hike was not mistaken for the end of tightening because markets still expected more
  • On November 10 she backed further gradual hikes, saying policy needs to be somewhat restrictive
  • She named three triggers for faster action: rising inflation expectations, building wage pressures and higher underlying inflation
  • Markets widely expect a quarter-point hike to 4.00% to 4.25% at the December 8 to 9 meeting

Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson stayed away from any near-term guidance on interest rates on Thursday. In a speech in New York, she argued that the Fed communicates best when the public understands how it thinks, not when officials spell out what comes next. With no fresh steer ahead of the December 8 to 9 meeting, her policy views from earlier this month remain the best guide to how she is likely to vote.

Speaking to the Money Marketeers of New York University, Paulson said understanding matters more than the particular ways the Fed communicates. If markets grasp the Fed’s reaction function, she argued, officials need to say less each time new data arrive, and policy can stay steady and largely predictable. She said the value of rate-path guidance depends on circumstances and is less useful in normal times, though Fed communications should still be clear about officials’ views.

She pointed to October as an example. The Fed held rates steady after hiking in September, but markets still expected further tightening, so the pause did not leave policy behind. In her words, shared understanding allowed policy to move deliberately, “without the risk that a pause was mistaken for a stop.” That was the closest she came to a signal: the October hold was a breather, not the end of the cycle.

Her remarks fit a wider debate inside the Fed. Under Chair Kevin Warsh, the central bank has shortened its policy statement and set up a task force on communications. Warsh himself has largely stepped back from giving rate guidance, even as many other officials continue to share their views.

Paulson had already shared hers. In a speech on November 10, she said policy needs to be somewhat restrictive to return inflation to 2% and that further gradual rate hikes seemed appropriate. She judged underlying inflation to be stuck between 2.5% and 3%. She also named three developments that would lead her to favour moving faster: inflation expectations drifting higher, wage pressures building, or underlying inflation rising. At the same time, she flagged that recent swings in stocks and oil could make consumer spending less durable than expected, one reason she prefers a gradual pace.

Read together, the two speeches point the same way. Paulson is a voter this year, and nothing in either speech suggests she would resist the quarter-point hike in December that markets widely expect, which would lift the target range to 4.00% to 4.25%. Thursday’s message adds that a slower pace should not be mistaken for a softer resolve. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin hits lowest since July as Fed hike talk and a Wall Street rout collide
item.description:
The rates message (like this: J.P. Morgan now sees three straight Fed hikes, dropping its ‘December and done’ call ) is hitting the whole crypto complex, not just Bitcoin. Ether dropped below $1,800 and sentiment gauges sit at extremes. Spot ETF products traded lower with the underlying, and IBIT and FBTC each fell less than 1% on the day. That leaves crypto equities such as COIN and MSTR, and listed miners, exposed to both falling token prices and a weaker tech tape. Bitcoin is trading as a high-beta risk asset rather than a hedge, so equity volatility and Fed pricing remain the main drivers for now.

---
